It usually runs a touch smaller than the nearby Washout and tends to be less crowded. On its better days it breaks further outside with cleaner form and longer lines, but most sessions are ordinary beachbreak surf.

guideSummary.surfnerd: 10th Street is a sand-bottomed beachbreak in Avalon that peels both left and right. It sits along the stretch from 8th Street to 16th Street, which picks up northeast swell and seems to amplify it, throwing up hollow peaks around the buried jetties.
guideSummary.surfForecast: 10th Street (Avalon) in New Jersey is a quite exposed beach/Jetty break that only works once in a while. Winter is the best time of year for surfing here. Sometimes crowded. Beware of rips and jellyfish.

It serves up both rights and lefts, and can definitely get fun on the right day.

guideSummary.surfForecast: 17th Street Boardwalk in Georgia is an exposed beach/Pier break that has reasonably consistent surf and can work at any time of the year. Best around mid tide. Rarely crowded here. Beware of rips, rocks, locals and sharks.

Expect a right-hander peeling over a sand bottom.

guideSummary.surfnerd: 26th to 30th Street Pier serves up fun rights and lefts over a sand bottom, mixing beach, pier, and jetty setups that pick up a range of swells. On a big northeast swell, powerful lefts peel down from the north end of the beach, and the north side of the 30th Street Pier keeps working all day through the summer.

guideSummary.surfnerd:
Overview

7th Street is a sand-bottomed beach and jetty break in Ocean City, and when it's on it arguably serves up the best left in town. Rights and lefts both break here: swells jack up off the 7th Street jetty, throwing out farther than they are high, then wall up and peel off more sanely down the rest of the beach. It shows its full potential from head-high to double-overhead, with big lefts rolling off the north jetty during a nor'easter and a decent right off the south jetty on a good southerly swell.

Ideal winds are from the northwest. Windswells and groundswells in equal measure and the best swell direction is from the southeast. When the surf is up, it can get quite busy in the water. Beware of Man-made danger (buoys etc..) and pollution.

The water here is probably the cleanest on the Outer Banks, and the peaks turn on and off with the sand, so it rewards a surfer willing to look rather than pull over at the first pack of cars.

It's often crowded here. Dangerous rips are a hazard of surfing here.

Nearby Trailer Park adds steep rights alongside hollow beachbreaks, plus a right and left that break over boulders in front of a small creek runout.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Ossabaw Island sits on Georgia's third largest barrier island, where catching a wave is a rare event. guideSummary.surfnerd: Picnic Tables is a peaky beach break along Patrick Air Force Base, one of a cluster of waves that also includes First and Second Light and Hangers. The bottom is mostly sand with the occasional rock, and this stretch marks the first signs of coquina, the reef-like sedimentary rock that runs south toward Indialantic. It is not especially hollow, but it is fast and racy, and it can barrel toward the inside on bigger days.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Rockaways is the closest consistently surfable spot to New York City, and the most popular day trip for city surfers. A long jetty sets up a hollow takeoff that peels into fast, grinding left walls over a sand bottom, and good lefts turn up often enough to make it genuinely fun. It is easy to reach on the subway, and the west-end towns of Breezy Point and Bell Harbor are pleasant areas with excellent surf.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Wolf Island is a National Wildlife Refuge made up of three islands, with Wolf sitting as the front island. It's reachable only by boat and sits a little farther back than Sapelo, so it gets somewhat shadowed on northeast or southeast swells while still working on most easterly ones. The wave breaks over sand as a beach break that peels both right and left.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Wooden Jetties is a punchy left that breaks over sand in the Holgate Wildlife Reserve, near the southern tip of Long Beach Island. A slight bend in the coast here lets the spot hold the biggest northeast swells, and the waves break below sea level with plenty of power.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Wooden Jetties in New Jersey is a fairly exposed beach/Jetty break that has fairly consistent surf and can work at any time of the year. Works best in offshore winds from the northwest. Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the ideal swell direction is from the northeast. The beach breaks are all lefts. Best around mid tide. When the surf is up, it can get quite busy in the water. Beware of rips,rusty wrecks.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Avalon Pier is a sand-bottomed beachbreak on North Carolina's Northern Outer Banks that peels both left and right around the pilings. The south side is usually the pick, though the north side has produced its share of memorable days. It can flip overnight from a closed-out, wishy-washy mushburger to a sand-sucking run of barrels, yet through all of that it stays remarkably consistent, both consistently rideable and consistently packed.

guideSummary.surfnerd: A Street is a sand-bottomed beach break in Saint Augustine, a short drive south of the pier and past 16th Street. It throws both rights and lefts, and the wave is a rolling, long ride that's easy to enjoy. Quality comes and goes with the sand, but when the banks line up it's a fun, decent setup.
